extracted.intended_audience: U.S. patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and applicants (attorneys/agents)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating and responding to rejections under 35 U.S.C. §103 (obviousness), including how to treat prior art, analogous art, applicant rebuttal evidence, and claim-as-a-whole analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.111(b) — Applicant reply/required traverse
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant must distinctly and specifically point out the supposed errors in the Office’s action and reply to every ground of objection and rejection in the Office action. The reply must present arguments pointing out the specific distinction believed to render the claims patentable over any applied references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant disagrees with factual findings, an effective traverse must include a reasoned statement explaining why the applicant believes the Office has erred as to the factual findings. A mere statement that the Office has not established a prima facie case or that reliance on common knowledge is unsupported by documentary evidence is not substantively adequate under 37 CFR 1.111(b). Examiners may repeat the prior rejection and make the next Office action final if traverse is inadequate (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of applicant’s rebuttal evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Office personnel should consider all timely rebuttal evidence submitted by applicants when reevaluating any obviousness determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rebuttal evidence may include secondary considerations (e.g., commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others) and evidence of unexpected results. Examples of applicant demonstrations include: (A) one of ordinary skill could not have combined the claimed elements by known methods (technological difficulties); (B) elements in combination do not merely perform the same function they perform separately; (C) the results of the claimed combination were unexpected. Once rebuttal evidence is presented, the Office should reconsider the obviousness determination in view of the entire record, review all rejections and bases for continued viability, and clearly communicate findings and conclusions. Follow MPEP §706.07(a) and MPEP §2145; consider affidavits/declarations under 37 CFR 1.132 per MPEP §716–§716.10.

rubrics_metrics.name: Availability of prior art under §102 for use in §103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Subject matter that is prior art under 35 U.S.C. §102 can be used to support a rejection under 35 U.S.C. §103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admitted prior art can be relied upon for anticipation or obviousness regardless of statutory category. A 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection may be based on references applicable under various §102 subsections (e.g., 102(a)(1), 102(a)(2), pre-AIA 102(a), 102(b), 102(e), etc.). Mechanisms such as affidavits/declarations to swear behind a reference (37 CFR 1.131) may apply depending on the reference type. See related MPEP sections (§901–§901.06(d), §2121–§2129, §2151–§2155).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive content of the prior art (what the prior art teaches/supports)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the substantive content of prior art with respect to issues like availability of inoperative devices, whether the prior art must be enabling, broad disclosures vs preferred embodiments, and admissions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §2121–§2129 for relevant case law. Examiner must evaluate whether the prior art would have taught, suggested, or made enabling the claimed subject matter to a person of ordinary skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal scope of prior art content — determine content at time invention was made
rubrics_metrics.description: Content of the prior art must be determined as of the time the invention was made to avoid impermissible hindsight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners/decisionmakers should 'cast the mind back' to what a person skilled in the art knew at the relevant time. See MPEP §2145 (discussion of rebutting hindsight-based rejections) and cases such as W.L. Gore & Associates v. Garlock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA §103(c) — applicant burden to show conditions apply
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant subject to pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 who wants to rely on pre-AIA §103(c) benefits bears the burden of establishing that the subject matter used in a §103 rejection and the claimed invention were, at the time the invention was made, owned by or subject to assignment to the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For joint research agreement benefits under pre-AIA §103(c) (applicable to certain pending dates), the applicant must establish: (A) the claimed invention was made by or on behalf of parties to a joint research agreement in effect on/before the invention date; (B) the invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of that agreement; and (C) the application discloses or is amended to disclose the parties to the agreement. See MPEP §706.02(l)(1)–(l)(2) and cited case law (e.g., Ex parte Yoshino, In re Bartfeld).

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art requirement for use in §103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: To rely on a reference under 35 U.S.C. §103, the reference must be analogous prior art to the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A reference is analogous if: (1) it is from the same field of endeavor as the claimed invention (even if addressing a different problem); or (2) it is reasonably pertinent to the problem faced by the inventor. 'Reasonably pertinent' means the reference would have logically commended itself to an inventor addressing the problem. Examiner may include a statement of understanding of the problem and should consider the specification and inferences a person of ordinary skill would draw. See KSR, In re Bigio, In re Icon Health & Fitness, and In re Klein for guidance and tests. Applicant arguments that a reference is nonanalogous should be fully considered in light of the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of similarities and differences in structure and function for analogy
rubrics_metrics.description: When deciding analogy, similarities and differences in structure and function of the inventions carry significant weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Office classification and cross-references are evidence but courts give greater weight to structural/functional similarities (see In re Ellis). Examiners should analyze structural/functional overlap when determining whether a reference is analogous art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy in the chemical arts — cross-field relevance
rubrics_metrics.description: In the chemical arts, references from apparently different subfields can be analogous when they address common chemical problems (e.g., absorbing biologically active materials, dye chemistry).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples from case law (Ex parte Bland, Stratoflex, In re Mlot-Fijalkowski) showing when teachings from different chemical or material contexts would reasonably be considered by an artisan addressing the inventor's problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy in the mechanical arts — broad inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: In simple mechanical inventions, a broad spectrum of prior art should be explored; it is reasonable to inquire into other areas where one of ordinary skill would be aware similar problems exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (e.g., Stevenson v. ITC, In re Bigio, In re Deminski) show that structural/function similarities (e.g., toothbrush vs hair brush) can render art analogous. Examiner should consider whether a person skilled in the mechanical art would look to other areas for solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy in the electrical arts — functional problem focus
rubrics_metrics.description: In electrical arts, references addressing similar functional problems (e.g., rate-limiting) may be analogous even if not in the same precise field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: circuits from high-power, high-frequency devices may be pertinent to cardiac pacemaker rate-limiting issues (Medtronic v. Cardiac Pacemakers). Examiners should consider whether the problem faced would lead an ordinary artisan to consult the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogy in the design arts — same general use requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: For design patents, a prior design is of the type claimed if it has the same general use as that claimed in the design application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court and Board decisions (e.g., In re Rosen, Ex parte Pappas, In re Butera) illustrate when furniture designs or feed bunk designs are analogous or nonanalogous depending on general use and designer's scope of knowledge. See MPEP §1504.03 for more.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differences between prior art and claimed invention — consider claim and prior art as whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascertaining differences between the prior art and the claims requires interpreting claim language and considering both the invention and the prior art references as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The §103 inquiry is whether the claimed invention 'as a whole' would have been obvious, not whether individual differences would have been obvious. See relevant claim interpretation law (MPEP §2111–§2116.01) and cases (Stratoflex, Schenck, In re Hirao) illustrating how admitted unobvious portions can make the combination nonobvious when viewed as a whole.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not distill the invention to a 'gist' or 'thrust' — respect 'as a whole' requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing an invention to a single gist or thrust disregards the statutory requirement to analyze the subject matter 'as a whole.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid narrowing consideration to one advantage or isolated limitation (see W.L. Gore, Bausch & Lomb, Jones v. Hardy, Panduit). Examiners must consider all claim limitations and the entire claimed combination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery of the source/cause of a problem can be part of the 'as a whole' inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: The discovery of the source or cause of a problem may itself be patentable subject matter even if the remedy is obvious once the source is identified; this discovery is part of the 'as a whole' analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, if prior art already contains the same solution for a similar problem, discovery of the source will not necessarily render the claimed subject matter patentable (see In re Sponnoble, In re Wiseman). Examiners should evaluate whether the prior art taught the same solution for a similar problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicants alleging discovery of a problem source must provide substantiating evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants who claim they discovered the source of a problem must substantiate that allegation with evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantiation may be by affidavit or declaration or by clear and persuasive assertions in the specification. Unsubstantiated attorney argument is insufficient (see In re Wiseman, In re Kaslow). Examiners should require appropriate support for such allegations.
